chapters.title: Fine-Tuning vs RAG vs In-Context
chapters.summary: The corporate decision matrix: when to prompt, when to retrieve, and when to train.

sections.title: Level 1: In-Context Prompting (Fastest & Cheapest)
sections.body:
When enterprise teams want to build custom AI, their immediate assumption is often that they need to 'train their own model'. In modern AI engineering, this is almost always the wrong first step. The first tier of customization—and the place where 80% of business problems should be solved—is In-Context Prompting.

In-Context Prompting simply means passing your specific instructions, tone guidelines, and examples directly in the system prompt at runtime. You do not touch the model's underlying weights. Modern foundation models have massive 'context windows' (e.g., Claude can ingest hundreds of pages of text in a single prompt).

This approach requires zero infrastructure, zero data science pipelines, and zero maintenance. You just write clear English instructions and embed your data. If you want the AI to write emails that sound like your CEO, you just paste 5 of the CEO's past emails into the prompt and say 'Mimic this style'. Engineers should only move past this level if they hit strict latency constraints, cost barriers, or complex logic that prompting simply cannot fix.
keyPoints: In-context prompting solves the vast majority of AI use cases without retraining models.
It leverages large context windows to inject data and rules directly at runtime.
It is the fastest, cheapest, and most maintainable way to customize AI behavior.
sections.example: A legal tech startup wants an AI to summarize contracts. Instead of spending $50,000 fine-tuning a custom legal model, they just write a massive system prompt containing their strict summarization rules and pass the 20-page contract in the API call. It works perfectly on day one.
sections.misconception: Common mistake: Assuming 'prompt engineering' is just a gimmick. In reality, writing highly structured, programmatic system prompts with JSON schemas and Few-Shot examples is a rigorous engineering discipline that replaces the need for fine-tuning in most apps.
sections.analogy: Think of it like getting a brilliant chef to cook your family recipe. You don't need to send the chef back to culinary school for 4 years to learn it (Fine-Tuning). You just hand them the recipe card right before they start cooking (In-Context Prompting).

sections.title: Level 2: RAG (Dynamic & Factual Knowledge)
sections.body:
If In-Context Prompting is so powerful, why move to Level 2? The limitation of standard prompting is scale. If you are building an AI to answer questions across your company's entire 10,000-page knowledge base, you physically cannot paste all 10,000 pages into the prompt every time a user asks a single question. It would exceed the model's token limit, take 30 seconds to process, and cost hundreds of dollars per query.

This is where Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) becomes mandatory. RAG acts as a dynamic filter. Instead of stuffing the entire knowledge base into the prompt, the system uses a Vector Database to instantly search the 10,000 pages, extract only the three paragraphs relevant to the user's specific question, and injects only those three paragraphs into the prompt.

RAG is the industry standard for any application that relies on large, complex, or frequently changing datasets. Because the knowledge is stored in an external database rather than baked into the AI, updating your company's policy just requires updating a database row, not retraining a neural network.
keyPoints: RAG is required when your dataset is too massive to fit inside a single prompt.
It dynamically fetches only the relevant facts and injects them at runtime.
It allows you to update the AI's knowledge base instantly without retraining.
sections.example: An e-commerce site has 500,000 changing products. They can't put the whole catalog in a prompt. When a user asks 'Do you have waterproof tents under $100?', the RAG system queries the database, retrieves the 4 matching tent listings, and feeds just those 4 into the LLM to generate a personalized response.
sections.misconception: Common mistake: Fine-tuning a model to teach it your company's proprietary facts. Neural networks are terrible at memorizing raw facts accurately. If you want the model to know specific data, use RAG. If you want it to learn a specific style or format, use Fine-Tuning.
sections.analogy: Think of it like a lawyer preparing for trial. Level 1 (Prompting) is carrying all the case files in your briefcase. Level 2 (RAG) is having a massive filing cabinet in the back room, and an assistant who runs back and hands you the exact folder you need right as the judge asks a question.

sections.title: Level 3: Fine-Tuning & LoRA (Style, Format & Tone)
sections.body:
If RAG handles knowledge, what is Fine-Tuning for? Fine-Tuning is Level 3, used exclusively when you need to fundamentally alter the behavior, tone, or output format of a model in ways that prompting cannot reliably achieve. Fine-tuning actually opens up the model and mathematically adjusts its internal weights based on thousands of examples you provide.

For instance, if you want an open-source model to output a highly specific, complex, nested JSON structure for thousands of medical records, standard prompting might fail 10% of the time. By fine-tuning the model on 5,000 perfect examples of that exact JSON structure, the model deeply learns the syntax.

Historically, fine-tuning was incredibly expensive, requiring updates to billions of parameters. Today, engineers use LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation). Instead of updating the entire massive model, LoRA freezes the main brain and just trains a tiny 'adapter'—a small matrix of weights that attaches to the model. This allows developers to fine-tune massive models on a single GPU in hours, drastically lowering the barrier to custom AI.
keyPoints: Fine-tuning mathematically alters the model's weights to teach it style, format, and tone.
It should NOT be used to teach the model new factual knowledge (use RAG for that).
LoRA makes fine-tuning vastly cheaper by only updating a tiny subset of the model's parameters.
sections.example: GitHub Copilot doesn't just use RAG. Microsoft fine-tuned the underlying models on billions of lines of code. The model physically altered its neural pathways to deeply understand syntax, indentation, and logic flow across dozens of programming languages, allowing it to generate code flawlessly.
sections.misconception: Common mistake: Assuming you need millions of data points to fine-tune. With modern techniques like LoRA, you can effectively fine-tune a model to adopt a specific tone or JSON format with just 500 to 1,000 highly curated, high-quality examples.
sections.analogy: Think of it like training a musician. RAG is handing a classically trained pianist sheet music for a jazz song—they can play it, but it might sound rigid. Fine-tuning is sending them to a jazz conservatory for a year until the swinging rhythm becomes permanently baked into their muscle memory.

# Need new facts / changing docs? -> Use RAG
# Need specific tone / complex formatting / lower latency? -> Fine-Tune (LoRA)
# Need quick prototype / few examples? -> In-Context Prompting

chapters.title: Agentic AI & Tool Use (ReAct & MCP)
chapters.summary: The frontier: autonomous multi-step reasoning, tool APIs, and workflows.

sections.title: The ReAct Loop: Thought, Action, Observation
sections.body:
Historically, LLMs were strictly conversational: you ask a question, they return text, and the interaction ends. Agentic AI fundamentally breaks this limitation, giving models the ability to execute tasks over time. The core architecture that enables this autonomy is the ReAct loop (Reasoning and Acting).

Instead of generating a final answer immediately, a ReAct agent operates in a continuous loop. First, it generates a 'Thought', breaking down the user's goal into a logical plan. Second, it generates an 'Action', deciding to trigger an external tool (like a web search or a Python script) to gather information. Third, it receives an 'Observation', reading the results that the tool returned.

The agent then loops back to step one. It uses the new observation to update its reasoning, plans its next action, and fires another tool. This loop continues autonomously until the agent determines it has fully satisfied the user's original request. This fundamentally transforms the LLM from a passive answering machine into an active, autonomous worker capable of solving multi-step problems.
keyPoints: Agents move beyond static text generation by autonomously looping through steps.
The ReAct framework dictates a cycle of Thought (plan), Action (execute tool), and Observation (analyze result).
The loop only terminates when the agent successfully verifies the final goal is met.
sections.example: A user asks an agent, 'What is the weather in Paris, and email me packing advice.' The Agent thinks: 'I need weather first.' Action: Calls Weather API. Observation: It's raining. Thought: 'Now I need to send the email.' Action: Calls Gmail API with rain advice. Observation: Email sent. Thought: 'Task complete.'
sections.misconception: Common mistake: Assuming the LLM itself is running the loop. The LLM is just a text generator; the 'loop' is actually a Python while-loop written by a developer orchestrating the calls to the LLM and the external APIs.
sections.analogy: Think of it like a chef in a kitchen. Thought: 'I need to make soup, but I don't know if the broth is hot.' Action: Tastes the broth. Observation: 'It's cold.' Thought: 'I need to turn up the heat.' Action: Turns dial. They loop this process until the soup is perfect.

sections.title: Function Calling & Tool Execution
sections.body:
For an AI agent to take an 'Action' in the real world, it needs a bridge between human language and backend code. This bridge is called 'Function Calling' (or Tool Use).

As a developer, you write a standard function in your backend—like `execute_sql(query)` or `charge_credit_card(amount)`. You then provide the LLM with a strictly typed JSON Schema that describes exactly what this function does and what arguments it requires. When the user asks the agent to perform a task, the LLM realizes it needs outside help. Instead of responding with conversational English, the model intelligently halts and outputs a highly structured JSON object, requesting to call your function with specific parameters.

Crucially, the AI itself does not execute code. It has no hands. It simply generates the JSON request. Your backend intercepts this JSON, safely executes the Python/Node code on your secure servers, and then feeds the resulting data back into the LLM as an 'Observation'. This strict separation of concerns keeps your infrastructure secure while giving the AI unlimited capabilities.
keyPoints: Function Calling allows an LLM to reliably trigger external code and APIs.
Developers provide JSON schemas defining the available tools; the LLM outputs JSON requesting a call.
The LLM never runs code directly; your backend executes the code and returns the result.
sections.example: A user says to a shopping AI, 'Buy the blue shoes.' The AI outputs a JSON object: {"tool": "checkout", "args": {"item": "blue_shoes", "qty": 1}}. The backend Python server parses this, hits the Stripe API, charges the card, and hands the success receipt back to the AI.
sections.misconception: Common mistake: Believing that giving an AI a tool is a security risk because the AI will 'hack' your system. The AI cannot execute anything—it only generates text strings. Your backend code is in complete control of validating the arguments and executing actual database changes.
sections.analogy: Think of it like an executive sitting in a boardroom without a laptop. The executive (the LLM) cannot physically update a spreadsheet. Instead, they write a specific request on a piece of paper (the JSON object) and hand it to an assistant (your backend code) who actually types the data into the computer.

sections.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) & Multi-Agent Systems
sections.body:
As developers build more complex agents, managing dozens of API integrations becomes a massive bottleneck. Every company writes their own custom bridging logic for Slack, GitHub, and Postgres. To solve this, the industry introduced the Model Context Protocol (MCP). MCP is an open-source standard—similar to how USB standardizes hardware—that provides a universal language for AI models to connect to external data sources and tools.

With MCP, an agent can instantly connect to an MCP-compliant database or filesystem without the developer writing custom integration code. This standardization paves the way for Multi-Agent Systems. Instead of having one massive 'God Agent' trying to do everything, you build specialized micro-agents.

In a multi-agent system, a 'Manager Agent' talks to the user and breaks down the project. It then delegates the database work to a specialized 'SQL Agent' (connected via MCP to Postgres), and delegates the coding to a 'Python Agent' (connected via MCP to GitHub). These agents collaborate, debate, and pass JSON messages to each other, forming a digital assembly line that executes incredibly complex enterprise workflows.
keyPoints: MCP is an open standard that universally connects AI models to external tools and data.
Multi-agent systems replace single monolithic bots with specialized, collaborative micro-agents.
Agents can route tasks, delegate sub-problems, and review each other's work autonomously.
sections.example: A user asks to 'Analyze Q3 revenue and build a web dashboard.' The Manager Agent assigns the analysis to the Data Agent (which uses MCP to query Snowflake). Once done, it passes the data to the Code Agent, which writes the React code and pushes it to GitHub—all completely autonomously.
sections.misconception: Common mistake: Thinking multi-agent systems are sci-fi sentience. Under the hood, they are just traditional microservice architectures, where the 'services' happen to be LLMs passing strictly typed JSON messages back and forth over standard HTTP protocols.
sections.analogy: Think of it like building a house. You don't hire one person to do the plumbing, electrical, and framing simultaneously. You hire a General Contractor (Manager Agent) who delegates the pipes to the plumber and the wires to the electrician, managing their communication until the house is finished.

    action = agent.decide_tool(thought)

Remove this future-derived feature and re-evaluate.

options: Compare with a baseline on representative unseen data.
Assume more memory means better reasoning.
